Line numbers refer to that file. Ranked below; the first is the one I'd fix.

**1. Digest credentials leak to any host that answers a redirect with a 4xx. Fix this first.**
`HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401` (lines 241-283) rebuilds the request and re-sends it with a fresh `Authorization` header (lines 273-276) to whatever URL the prepared request currently points at, with no check that the host still matches the one the user authenticated to. The hook is registered in `__call__` (lines 299-300) and survives redirects, because the session copies the prepared request between hops with its hooks attached. The session's cross-host stripping of the static `Authorization` header doesn't help: the hook re-adds it after the new host answers. Line 250 widens the trigger from 401 to any 4xx, and `handle_redirect` (lines 236-239) resets the one-shot counter on every hop, re-arming the resend across a whole redirect chain. Net effect: host A bounces you to hostile host B, B issues its own Digest challenge, and the client answers with a response derived from the real password. With MD5 (the default, see #3) that response is offline-crackable, so B ends up with the username and a brute-force target.

**2. Server-controlled challenge values are spliced into the Authorization header unescaped.**
`HTTPDigestAuth.build_digest_header` (lines 221-232) assembles the header with f-strings: `username`, `realm`, and `nonce` at line 222, `opaque` at line 226, `algorithm` at line 228. None are quoted or escaped. A challenge value containing `"` or `,` breaks out of the quoted-string and injects or overrides parameters in the header; the username at line 222 is caller-controlled and does the same. A malicious server or on-path attacker can make the client assert Digest parameters it never agreed to, which matters most when a proxy or gateway parses that header downstream.

**3. The server picks the hash, the client has no floor, and failure is silent.**
`build_digest_header` defaults to MD5 when the challenge omits `algorithm` (lines 138-139), accepts MD5 and MD5-SESS (lines 143-150) plus SHA-1 (lines 151-158), and takes whatever `algorithm` string the challenge carries. An on-path attacker downgrades the exchange to MD5 by stripping the parameter. When the algorithm or qop is unsupported, the function returns `None` (lines 178-179, 215-216); `handle_401` then assigns that `None` as the header value (lines 273-275), which drops the header and sends the request unauthenticated instead of failing loudly.

Also noted, below the cut: `_basic_auth_str` (lines 35-53) silently coerces non-string credentials with `str()`, so a bytes password is sent as its Python repr, and non-latin-1 credentials raise at lines 56-60; `__eq__` on both auth classes (lines 83-92, 305-314) compares passwords with `==` rather than a constant-time comparison.
